hints: Notice the question tells you energy is released, so start by reminding yourself what exothermic really means for the surroundings.
Remember the two energy steps in any reaction, breaking bonds always takes energy in while forming bonds always gives energy out.
For a net release of energy, compare the sizes of those two steps and ask which one must be larger.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the energy change**

Think of this like a bank balance. Energy is released to the surroundings, so the reaction is exothermic with a negative enthalpy change.

$$\Delta H = -55 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Recall the bond energy rule**

Every chemical change does both things. Old bonds like $\text{O-H}$ must be broken, which costs energy, and new bonds like in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are formed, which pays energy back.

$$\Delta H = \text{energy taken in to break bonds} - \text{energy given out to form bonds}$$

**Decide which side is bigger**

For $\Delta H$ to be negative, the payback must be bigger than the cost. More energy is given out when new bonds form than is taken in to break old bonds, so there is a net release.

options.A: Incorrect. Bond breaking alone can never make a reaction exothermic because breaking bonds always absorbs energy. This reaction also forms new bonds, especially $\text{H-O}$ in water.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true that bond forming releases energy, but it is not the only process. Old $\text{O-H}$ and other bonds must first be broken, which takes energy in.
options.C: Incorrect. This reverses the energy logic. Breaking bonds takes energy in, it does not give energy out. If breaking cost more than forming paid back, the reaction would be endothermic.
options.D: Correct. This is the definition of exothermic in bond energy terms. The energy released in forming new bonds, mainly to make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in neutralisation, is greater than the energy absorbed to break the acid $\text{O-H}$ bond.
